## FCRA and Your NGO Website: What to Publish, What to Capture and How to Keep FC-4 Easy

If your NGO receives foreign contribution, an NGO website built around FCRA needs to do three things: publish the audited foreign-contribution accounts that the FCRA Rules require on your official website, keep a clear and current compliance page that matches your registration, and capture the donor data at the point of donation that your annual return in Form FC-4 will later ask for. The first is a legal duty with a nine-month clock. The second is good practice that regulators and donors both check. The third is the one most organisations skip, and it is why FC-4 season becomes a scramble through email inboxes in December.

This article was rewritten from our earlier checklist of FC-4 filing steps. Filing the return itself is work for your accounts team and chartered accountant, and nothing here is legal or tax advice. What we can usefully cover, as a Pune web development team that builds NGO donation platforms, is the website side: what has to be published and where, how a donation flow should be structured so the data is already tidy, and how to run the page without it quietly going stale. One point deserves care up front, because many NGO websites still get it wrong: the quarterly receipts table that older guides tell you to display is no longer required, and we explain below what changed.

### What an FC-4 return is, in two paragraphs

Form FC-4 is the annual return in which an FCRA-registered association reports foreign contribution received, transferred and used in a financial year. Rule 17 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2011 requires it to be filed online, with scanned copies of the income and expenditure statement, the receipt and payment account and the balance sheet, and requires it to be certified by a chartered accountant. The due date is within nine months of the close of the financial year, which for the 1 April to 31 March year means around 31 December. Even an association that received nothing in the year files a nil return, although the rule says the accounts and certificate need not be attached in that case ([The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules, 2011, as reproduced on Indian Kanoon](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/20690064/); check the live text on the official FCRA portal before relying on any detail).

That is the filing. The website connects to it in two ways. Rule 13 separately requires the audited accounts to be published on your own site, and the quality of your FC-4 depends heavily on records that are either captured cleanly at donation time or reconstructed painfully months later. Both are website and process problems before they are accounting problems.

## What the FCRA Rules actually require you to publish on the website

### The annual accounts requirement (Rule 13(a))

Rule 13(a), as substituted in December 2015, requires an association that holds an FCRA registration or prior permission to publish its audited statement of accounts on the receipts and utilisation of foreign contribution for each financial year on its official website, or on a website specified by the Central Government. The statements are the income and expenditure statement, the receipt and payment account and the balance sheet, and the deadline is within nine months of the close of the financial year ([Indian Kanoon text of the Rules](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/20690064/)).

Two practical consequences follow for a website build:

- **The accounts must actually sit on a page.** A PDF emailed to the auditor, or uploaded only to the government portal, does not satisfy a rule that says official website. If your NGO has no website, the rule contemplates a government-specified site; ask your compliance adviser which applies to you.
- **The nine-month clock mirrors FC-4.** For the year ending 31 March, the same 31 December date generally governs both the return and the publication. Putting both on one internal calendar entry prevents one being done without the other.

### The quarterly receipts table is no longer required

Until mid-2022, Rule 13(b) also required quarterly details of foreign contribution received, with donor names, amounts and dates, to be published within fifteen days of the end of each quarter. Many NGO websites still carry a table titled "Quarterly FCRA receipts", and many agency guides and templates still recommend it.

That clause was omitted by the Ministry of Home Affairs by notification G.S.R. 506(E) dated 1 July 2022, so the quarterly display is no longer a legal requirement on your website or on the FCRA portal. The requirement to publish annual audited accounts remained ([Harchandani and Associates: Important FCRA amendments applicable from 1 July 2022](https://harchandani.in/articles/important-fcra-amendments-applicable-from-1st-july-2022); [FMSF India: quarterly receipts display no longer required](https://www.fmsfindia.org.in/news/do-you-released-on-fcra-registered-entities-need-not-require-to-display-the-quarterly-receipts-of-fc-donation-on-the-website)). We checked this against two compliance sources and a third summary; the Gazette notification itself is the authority, and TODO: confirm with your CA that no later notification changes the position for your registration category.

What should you do with an old quarterly page? Do not simply delete it overnight. Ask your adviser whether to retain historical tables as an archive, label them clearly with the period they cover, and stop promising "updated quarterly" in the page copy. A page that claims to be current but stopped updating in 2022 is a worse signal than no page. Equally, many NGOs choose to keep voluntary donor-category summaries because they build trust; that is a choice, not a mandate, and the individual donor names of foreign contributors are a privacy and security decision to take deliberately with legal advice.

### The 2026 amendments add digital-presence disclosure

The Ministry's June 2026 amendments to the FCRA Rules bring the website itself into the compliance record: reporting coverage describes new requirements to declare the official website and social media accounts, disclose publications issued during the year, identify the ultimate foreign donor in some intermediary cases, and file a new Form FC-6F for activity-specific registration by 21 June 2027 for existing registrants. We unpacked those in detail in [what the FCRA Amendment Rules 2026 require from your website](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-fcra-amendment-rules-2026/), which cites the reporting we relied on. For this article the relevant point is simple: the compliance page described below becomes more valuable, not less, because a mismatch between your website and your filings is now easier to spot.

## Designing the "FCRA and foreign contribution" page

A single dedicated page, linked from the footer, is the cleanest answer. It works for the regulator, the auditor, the foreign donor's due-diligence team and the curious supporter alike. Here is what belongs on it.

### Registration details that must be correct

- **Registered name and registration number.** Exactly as on your certificate. A trading name or abbreviation in place of the registered name creates avoidable doubt.
- **Registration validity.** State the current validity date, and update it the day a renewal is granted. If you are within a renewal window, say so factually rather than leaving an expired date up.
- **Registered address and designated bank.** Many NGOs publish the name of the designated FCRA bank and branch so that donors send money to the right account. Publish only what you are comfortable having public, and never publish account credentials or internal account details beyond what a donor needs to remit.
- **Registered purposes and areas.** Describe your activities in the language of your registration, and keep your programme pages consistent with it. After the 2026 amendments, a website that describes work outside your registered categories is a visible inconsistency.

### Annual accounts archive

Create a dated archive, one entry per financial year, each linking to the audited receipts and utilisation statements as downloadable PDFs. Use plain filenames that state the year, for example "FCRA audited accounts 2024-25", and show the publication date beside each. Keep older years available; removing history to look tidy is the opposite of transparency.

Technical details that matter more than people expect: make the PDFs text-searchable rather than scanned images, keep file sizes sensible so they open on a budget phone (see our note on [low-bandwidth mobile donors](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-low-bandwidth-mobile-donors-2026/)), and give each document a stable URL so a link in a donor's grant file keeps working next year. A year-by-year page is also straightforward to build into a [custom NGO website](/pages/ngopage) with a simple admin screen for adding a new year.

### Digital presence and publications

Given the 2026 direction of travel, list your official website domain and your active social media accounts in one place, and keep an annual report and newsletter archive. This mirrors what you declare to the Ministry and gives you a single source to check against. If an account is abandoned, close it rather than leaving it as an unexplained discrepancy. For the broader question of what to publish about outcomes and finances, see our guide to [transparency and impact reporting on an NGO website](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-transparency-impact-reporting-2026/).

### A plain statement for foreign donors

Foreign donors and their foundations frequently ask whether you are FCRA registered and how to remit. A short, factual paragraph answers it: registration status, the fact that foreign contribution is received only into the designated account, who to contact for remittance details, and which documents you can share on request. Avoid claims you cannot document, and avoid promising tax treatment in the donor's own country; that varies and is for the donor's adviser.

## Building a foreign-donor donation flow that keeps FC-4 tidy

The most expensive FC-4 problems are not filing mistakes. They are reconstruction problems: a payment arrives, nobody recorded which donor or purpose it related to, and months later a treasurer is matching bank lines to email threads. A donation flow designed with the annual return in mind removes most of that work. For the payment-gateway side of this, including the question of which routes can receive foreign money at all, read our guide on [setting up a payment gateway for an FCRA NGO](/blog/fcra-payment-gateway-setup-ngos/); this section covers the data design.

### Separate the foreign and domestic paths clearly

The FCRA framework expects foreign contribution to land in the designated FCRA account and to be tracked separately from domestic funds. On the website this usually means one of two designs:

- **A dedicated foreign-donor page or toggle** that routes to a gateway or remittance instructions suited to foreign money, kept visibly separate from the domestic Indian-rupee donation form.
- **A clear selector early in the flow** asking where the donor is based, with the foreign path leading to the right instructions and not to the domestic UPI form.

Whichever you use, test it as a real foreign donor would, with a foreign card or with the wire-transfer instructions. Do not assume the domestic form is safe to reuse. Whether a particular gateway may accept foreign-currency payments into your FCRA account is a compliance and banking question for your CA and bank, not something a plugin should decide on its own.

### Fields worth capturing at the moment of donation

None of these is a legal instruction; they are the fields that, in our experience of building donation systems, make later reporting far easier. Confirm the exact fields the portal and your adviser require, and capture only what you need under data-protection principles.

| Field | Why it helps later |
|---|---|
| Donor name and organisation | Matches the donor-wise entries your return needs |
| Country of donor | Distinguishes foreign from domestic quickly |
| Donor address | Often requested for donor-wise records |
| Amount and currency as paid | Keeps the original currency, not only the rupee figure |
| Date of receipt and bank reference | Lets the treasurer match the bank line |
| Purpose or programme chosen | Supports utilisation records by activity |
| Restricted or general | Flags earmarked funds that must be used for the stated purpose |
| Intermediary or platform, and underlying donor if known | Relevant to the ultimate-donor point in the 2026 amendments |
| Consent record | Evidence for how you may use the data |

Store the rupee value at the date of credit as reported by the bank, not an estimate from the day of donation; exchange rates move, and the bank credit is what your books will show. We deliberately do not tell you which exchange-rate rule applies; that is an accounting decision.

### Keep a monthly reconciliation export

The simplest habit with the largest payoff: a monthly export from the donation system listing every foreign receipt with the fields above, matched against the FCRA bank statement by the treasurer. Any mismatch is then a one-month problem, not a twelve-month one. The export can be a spreadsheet generated from the admin area. If your site cannot produce it, that is a feature to request before the next financial year begins, not after.

### Receipts and acknowledgements

Acknowledge each foreign receipt with a clear receipt or confirmation. Do not apply Indian tax-exemption wording, such as 80G certificates, to foreign donors by default; the rules for Indian tax receipts and for foreign remittances differ, and mixing them on one template is a frequent error. Have your CA approve the receipt wording for each donor category.

## Document hosting and security

Compliance documents are public-facing, but the data behind them is not. Separate the two deliberately.

- **Public folder.** Only final, audited, approved PDFs. Check each file's metadata and content before upload so that no internal comments, bank details or personal data of beneficiaries slip into a published file. PDF metadata and hidden text layers are a common leak.
- **Private store.** Grant agreements, donor correspondence, bank statements and working files should live in access-controlled storage, not in the website's media library, where files can often be reached by guessing the URL.
- **Retention.** Rule 17 requires accounting statements to be kept for six years, according to the text we reviewed; confirm the current period with your adviser and build the retention into your storage plan rather than relying on someone's laptop ([Indian Kanoon text of the Rules](https://indiankanoon.org/doc/20690064/)).
- **Access control.** Limit who can publish to the compliance page. Use named accounts with two-step sign-in, and remove access when someone leaves. Our guide to [securing a donation website](/blog/ngo-website-development-india-donation-site-security-hosting-2026/) covers hosting, backups and offboarding in depth.

## A year-round workflow, not a December scramble

Here is a rhythm that fits most small and mid-sized NGOs. Adjust it with your CA.

1. **Monthly:** export foreign receipts from the donation system and reconcile with the FCRA bank statement. Note unmatched items and chase the missing donor details at once.
2. **Quarterly:** a thirty-minute website check. Is the registration validity date current? Do the listed social accounts and website match what you declared? Are programme pages consistent with registered purposes? Is any new publication ready to archive?
3. **After year-end (April to June):** close the books, finalise donor-wise and purpose-wise summaries from your records, and hand the reconciled data to the auditor.
4. **Before 31 December:** your internal deadline should fall weeks earlier. Publish the audited foreign-contribution accounts on the website and file FC-4 in the same window, with the CA certificate agreeing with what you submit. A certificate that does not match the final entries is a common cause of delay.
5. **After filing:** update the accounts archive, record the filing date internally and set next year's calendar.

Assign a named owner for each step. A website compliance page with no owner is a page that goes stale within a year.

## Mistakes we see on NGO websites

- **A quarterly table that stopped updating.** Either archive it clearly or remove the promise of regular updates, after taking advice.
- **An expired registration date left online.** Visitors and donors read this as a lapsed registration even when renewal is under way.
- **Accounts published only on a government portal.** Rule 13(a) refers to your official website.
- **Scanned, unsearchable PDFs of 40 MB.** They fail on mobile data and are hard for due-diligence teams to review.
- **Domestic receipt templates sent to foreign donors.** Wording and tax references should differ.
- **Programme descriptions that exceed the registration.** Align the wording, or raise the matter with your adviser if the work really does fall outside your registered purposes.
- **No donor data captured at payment time.** The root cause of most reconstruction work later.

## What this does and does not replace

A well-built website does not file your return and does not make you compliant on its own. FC-4 is certified by a chartered accountant on the basis of your books and bank records. Exactly which FCRA obligations apply to you depends on your registration category, your funding structure and the notifications in force when you read this. The Ministry has amended the Rules repeatedly, and an article, including this one, can age. Treat the official FCRA portal and the Gazette as the authority, and your CA or FCRA consultant as the person who interprets them for you. Where this article says something is a recommendation rather than a rule, it is because it is a way we have seen organisations reduce risk, not because the law spells it out.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do I still have to publish quarterly FCRA receipts on my website?

No, not under the rules as amended. Rule 13(b), which required quarterly receipt details, was omitted by MHA notification G.S.R. 506(E) dated 1 July 2022. The requirement to publish annual audited accounts on your official website remains. Confirm your position with a chartered accountant.

### What FCRA documents must be published on an NGO website?

Rule 13(a) requires the audited statement of accounts on receipts and utilisation of foreign contribution for each financial year, comprising the income and expenditure statement, receipt and payment account and balance sheet, within nine months of the financial year closing. Publish them as dated, searchable PDFs on your official website.

### When is the FCRA annual return FC-4 due?

Within nine months of the close of the financial year, which for the year ending 31 March generally means 31 December. It is filed online, certified by a chartered accountant, and a nil return is still required if no foreign contribution was received. Check the portal for the current instructions.

### What donor data should a foreign donation page capture?

Typically the donor's name, country, address, amount and currency, date and bank reference, the purpose chosen and whether the gift is restricted. These make donor-wise and purpose-wise records far easier to prepare. Confirm required fields with your CA and collect only what you need under data-protection principles.
